Good morning. First, I want to thank Chair Joseph and the rest of the Council for allowing me to speak here today. My name is Hana Ira and I’m a high school junior in Queens. I’m also a youth advocate with the Asian American Student Advocacy Project’s Anti-bullying and Harassment Campaign. AASAP is CACF’s citywide youth leadership team. To improve school culture and climate, every school should have a restorative justice program. The funding for restorative justice in schools must be sustainable, not to disappear after one year, but a long-term investment to ensure that student are-students feel belonged and safe in school. In middle school I didn’t have any culturally restorative staff that I could turn to for support or just to talk to. I was one of the very few AAPI students of color in my grade. I was constantly mocked, called racial slurs, told my food smelled weird, and told that eating with my hands was gross. I was even asked if I was related to that one kid from the virus, referring to a Chinese American student in my grade. These

COMMITTEE ON FINANCE JOINTLY WITH COMMITTEE ON FINANCE 258 comments weren’t whispered. They were said aloud in hallways, in my classrooms, often in front of teachers and staff that did not care. I felt invisible and ashamed. Eventually, I stopped going to the lunchroom altogether because I couldn’t handle these comments and stares. I began eating in the bathroom just to feel safe. Over time, this isolation deeply affected my mental health. Without staff that could actually understand my background, I was left to believe that this normal, that staying silent was the only option. And I’m not the only one that experiences these instances. AAPI students across the City face microaggression, bullying and erasure, whether it’s mocking our names, making racial slurs, stereotyping us. They may not always be violent, but they deeply impact our sense of identity in school. I believe all students deserve to go to school feeling safe, being able to learn and thrive without fear and feeling welcomed. However, that is just not the case. These hurtful and harmful comments and judgements from both students and teachers are rooted in misunderstanding and lack of knowledge of each other. It is time for the City and schools to address this with solutions that center

First, training school staff to recognize anti-Asian bullying and biases. Second, school must intentionally create space for students to share their experiences and feedback. Our voices must be included in the process. Healing and justice takes time, but students deserve more than reactive discipline. We deserve to be seen, valid and cared for. Thank you.

Many AAPI students do not feel comfortable in schools due to racially discriminatory remarks as a consequence of stereotypes being perpetuated through a lack of an inclusive curriculum and culturally-sensitive staff. Students hear microaggressions and passively racist comments every day that have no repercussions. When a more severe racist remark is reported, traditional punishment like suspension will occur. However, this approach ignores the root causes of the issue and does not encourage those who caused harm to learn about the negative impact they affected. As a result, students will repeat discriminatory comments targeting the AAPI community with no real understanding of the depth of their actions.
